prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: asplenia (a severe immunocompromised state) and the left extensor plantar response (a focal neurological sign) are imaging-first criteria under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.

Do not attribute the acute deterioration to normal pressure hydrocephalus: fever, meningism and a neutrophilic CSF with a glucose ratio of 0.14 are not features of NPH, and any shunt decision waits until the meningitis is treated and the hydrocephalus is reassessed.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 (74 years), diabetes mellitus and asplenia (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of asplenia (a severe immunocompromised state) and a focal neurological sign (left extensor plantar response) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin (MIC 0.06 mg/L) and ceftriaxone (MIC 0.5 mg/L or less), so stop ampicillin and any vancomycin and continue ceftriaxone or switch to benzylpenicillin.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

differential.key_features: Supports: five weeks of shuffling small-step gait and cognitive decline, ventricular enlargement on prior imaging, communicating hydrocephalus with Evans index 0.37 and patent cisterns on CT. Against as the sole cause: fever, meningism, opening pressure 28 cm H2O and a neutrophilic CSF (380 cells, 68% neutrophils, protein 178 mg/dL, glucose ratio 0.14) with S. pneumoniae on PCR; communicating hydrocephalus is also a recognized complication of bacterial meningitis.
Raised by age 74, diabetes and asplenia, which make empirical cover necessary; excluded as the cause by Listeria not detected on PCR and S. pneumoniae on PCR and blood culture.
Excluded: neutrophilic pleocytosis with glucose ratio 0.14 and protein 178 mg/dL, S. pneumoniae on PCR; enterovirus, HSV, VZV and parechovirus not detected.
Excluded: HSV-1/2 PCR not detected, no seizures or temporal focal features, bacterial CSF pattern with an identified organism.
Against: acute neutrophilic rather than lymphocytic CSF, AFB stain and TB PCR negative, S. pneumoniae identified.
No thunderclap onset, no hemorrhage on CT, CSF clear of blood (RBC 2 cells/microL).

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of asplenia (a severe immunocompromised state) and a focal neurological sign (left extensor plantar response) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Fever, meningism and a neutrophilic CSF are not features of normal pressure hydrocephalus; communicating hydrocephalus is a recognized complication of bacterial meningitis, so a known or suspected NPH does not explain an acute febrile deterioration.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: asplenia (severe immunocompromised state) and a left extensor plantar response (focal neurological sign). NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (asplenia is an immunodeficiency outside its scope). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025).

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Soon-Ja Park is a 74-year-old right-handed Korean woman with a history of remote splenectomy for idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, lumbar disc herniation, and previously diagnosed mild cognitive impairment who presents to the emergency department with progressive confusion and worsening gait instability over the past ten days, with new-onset low-grade fever over the past two days. According to her husband, the patient first began to show noticeable decline in her gait approximately five weeks ago, developing a shuffling, small-step pattern with frequent stumbles and near-falls. She was seen at an outpatient neurology clinic three weeks ago, where her gait abnormalities and worsening memory difficulties raised concern for possible normal pressure hydrocephalus given her age and clinical presentation. Brain imaging at that visit was noted to show ventricular enlargement, and further workup was planned. However, over the past ten days, her cognitive function has deteriorated more rapidly than expected. She has become increasingly confused, forgetting the names of family members, repeating questions, and on two occasions becoming disoriented in her own apartment. Five days ago, she developed a mild cough and nasal congestion. Her husband took her to a local primary care clinic three days ago, where she was diagnosed with an upper respiratory infection and started on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Despite the antibiotic treatment, she developed a low-grade fever two days ago, measured at 38.1 degrees Celsius at home. She began complaining of a diffuse headache that was not relieved by acetaminophen. Yesterday evening, she became notably more lethargic, had difficulty staying awake during dinner, and vomited once. Her husband also observed that she seemed to flinch and turn away from bright lights. This morning, she was difficult to rouse from sleep and could only state her name when questioned. Her husband called emergency services. In the emergency department, she intermittently opens her eyes to voice and follows simple commands inconsistently. She complains of neck pain when asked.

neurological_exam.additional: Nuchal rigidity present — moderate resistance to passive neck flexion. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive — involuntary hip and knee flexion with passive neck flexion. No petechiae or purpura on skin examination. No lymphadenopathy. Small well-healed left upper quadrant surgical scar consistent with prior splenectomy.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, reactive to light but sluggish. Visual fields grossly intact to confrontation when patient cooperates. No gaze deviation. Mild bilateral facial grimace to stimulation, symmetric. No obvious facial droop. Fundoscopic exam limited by cooperation; no papilledema appreciated. Gag reflex intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Previously noted to have a shuffling, small-step gait with difficulty turning on prior clinic visits. Currently unable to stand unassisted due to somnolence and unsteadiness. Required wheelchair transport to the emergency department.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Drowsy but arousable to voice. Oriented to person only; confused about place and date. Unable to recall three words at five minutes. Speech is slow but coherent when she responds. Follows simple one-step commands inconsistently. Cannot perform serial subtractions. K-MMSE estimated at 15 (baseline 22 eighteen months ago). GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four extremities spontaneously but less vigorously than expected. Upper extremities: 4+/5 strength bilaterally in proximal and distal muscle groups, limited by cooperation. Lower extremities: 4/5 bilaterally, again limited by effort. No pronator drift assessable. No fasciculations or atrophy noted. Tone is mildly increased diffusely.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are extensor (upgoing) on the left and equivocal on the right.
